Memory.value: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns
Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory

Negative Appraisals.value: People are not what they seem
I feel isolated and set apart from others

vignette: Kaito's life was forever changed on a fateful day in August when a category 5 typhoon tore through his coastal hometown. The howling winds and relentless rain had seemed to last an eternity as he huddled with his family in their small apartment. The sounds of shattering glass, crumbling walls, and screams still echoed in his mind like they were yesterday. As the storm raged on, Kaito's neck was wrenched in a sudden gust, leaving him with a chronic ache that flared up without warning. It was these moments of pain that would often transport Kaito back to that day. The memory felt almost surreal – as if it had happened to someone else. He couldn't shake the feeling that he'd simply imagined the entire ordeal, that it was all just some macabre fantasy born from his own fevered imagination. And yet, every time the memory resurfaced, the taste of saltwater and mud flooded his senses, leaving him gasping for air. As Kaito struggled to reconcile the past with his present life in the city, he found himself increasingly withdrawn. His work as a UX designer was suffering – not because he couldn't focus, but because he felt like an outsider, looking in on the world through a distorted lens. People seemed fake, their smiles and laughter just thin veneers hiding darker intentions. He felt disconnected from his colleagues, his friends, even himself. Feeling physically unwell also became a regular occurrence – usually after a long night of working late or socializing with others. It was as if his body had become attuned to the slightest hint of stress, responding by making him feel queasy and lightheaded. Kaito began to avoid social gatherings, fearing that one wrong move would set off another panic attack. He couldn't explain why these small triggers – a neck pain here, a feeling of illness there – seemed to have such an outsize impact on his life. It was as if every event, no matter how minor, threatened to spiral him back into the heart of that storm. This feeling of being constantly on edge only served to further entrench Kaito's negative appraisals: people were not trustworthy; he didn't belong anywhere. Kaito started noticing how certain events – anniversaries of the typhoon, or news reports about natural disasters – would send him tumbling down a rabbit hole of memories and emotions. The anniversary was particularly fraught, as it coincided with a major design project deadline at work. Feeling overwhelmed by both past traumas and present responsibilities, Kaito lashed out at his colleagues during an important meeting. That incident marked the final straw – Kaito realized that he needed help to break this cycle of pain, memories, and isolation. As he sat in his dark apartment, nursing a wounded pride and a sore neck, Kaito knew it was time to confront the storm within him head-on.
